QUARTER 3 · MODULE 14 · 2-WEEK CYCLE
Ancient China — Blue-and-White Plate
Focus: PATTERN and COLOR (a limited blue-on-white palette), with Balance supporting via the round plate. Anchor: a real Willow-pattern plate (Mintons, c. 1850, Cooper Hewitt, public domain).
⚠️ HISTORICAL ACCURACY (teach honestly, do not blur)
• Chinese blue-and-white porcelain (cobalt-blue designs on white porcelain) is the genuine, ancient tradition, perfected in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 A.D.) and exported worldwide.
• The "Blue Willow" / Willow pattern (willow tree, bridge, house, two birds, plus a made-up romantic story) is a later English design, attributed to Josiah Spode and others around the 1790s A.D. It imitated Chinese export porcelain; it is not an ancient Chinese design.
• The lesson teaches both honestly: students study the Chinese blue-and-white tradition and the English Willow pattern it inspired. The student artwork lets them choose a willow-style scene or their own landscape, so they are not told the willow story is Chinese.

Made by Mintons (England), porcelain, c. 1850 A.D., held by the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum (acc. 1993-134-24). Public domain (published before 1931; Wikimedia PD Mark). Source: Wikimedia Commons, File:Blue Willow Plate, 19th century (CH 18643709).jpg — https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Blue_Willow_Plate,_19th_century_(CH_18643709).jpg . Three images are embedded from this one file: the full plate (anchor), a crop of the center willow scene (legend section), and a crop of the rim (the "quick look at pattern" detail).
• Note on this plate: it is a fancy gilded version (gold rim). The lesson states honestly that the willow scene itself, and most Willow china and the student project, is blue-on-white only, so the gold does not undercut the limited-palette focus.
• The legend (added this revision): Part 1 now tells the tragic Willow legend (Koong-se and Chang, the bridge, boat, island, and the two lovers turned into doves). It is framed honestly as a romantic tale invented by English sellers around 1800 to accompany the pattern, NOT an ancient Chinese story. See the Historical Accuracy box above. The reviewer-requested updates (See/Notice/Wonder, Quick Check, Watch It Work, and the quiz) all now reference the plate and legend.
• Focus: Element = Color (limited palette, blue on white); Principle = Pattern (repeating border + repeated motifs); Balance supports via the round plate.

🔑 QUIZ ANSWER KEY (teacher-facing — do not publish)
1. A — A shape with real depth that you can see from more than one side (form)
2. A — Symbolism
3. A — A symbol, often an animal, owned by a particular family or clan (crest)
4. A — Focal point
5. A — Haida, Tlingit, and Kwakwaka'wakw
6. True — a totem pole shows family crests and tells clan stories
7. False — totem poles are not objects of worship; they record families and stories
8. Matching — a shape with real depth = Form; an image that stands for an idea = Symbol; the spot your eye goes to first = Focal point; simplified into bold clear shapes = Stylized
📝 BUILD & SOURCE NOTES
• Image: the anchor is a historical photograph of totem poles at Howkan, Alaska, c. 1922 A.D. (source file Sternberg-TotempolesHowkan-ca 1922.jpg). As a c. 1922 photograph it is public domain; it is embedded as inline base64 in the content page so it renders without external files. The lesson describes only what is visible in the photograph (three carved poles, deep three-dimensional form, a large face acting as a focal point, an evergreen and plank house in the background) and does not attribute specific crest meanings to the individual figures, which are not identified in the source.
• Accuracy & respect: Totem poles are made by Pacific Northwest Coast peoples (such as the Haida, Tlingit, and Kwakwaka'wakw) of present-day British Columbia and Alaska. They are carved cedar monuments showing family crests and clan stories, not objects of worship. Each animal is a symbol of a family, story, or trait. WEEK 2 · ARTWORK + ARTIST STATEMENT
Mandala Design
Major Project · 100 pts · Due end of Week 2
📋 PROJECT OVERVIEW
Now you put pattern and radial balance to work in your own mandala. You will fold a circle into equal sections, design one section, and repeat that design evenly all the way around. When you finish, you will have a single balanced design that radiates from one center, just like the painted mandala you studied this week.
🎯 ELEMENTS & PRINCIPLES FOCUS
Principles of Design: Pattern, Radial Balance
Elements of Art (supporting): Line, Color
🛠️ WHAT YOU NEED
A round object to trace (a plate or bowl) · paper · pencil · eraser · scissors (optional) · 4 to 5 coloring tools (colored pencils, crayons, or markers) · a darker pencil or fine marker for outlining (optional)
📝 STEP-BY-STEP
1
Trace a large circle using a plate or bowl. Cut it out if you like, or leave it on the paper.
2
Fold the circle into equal sections. Fold it in half, then in half again to make fourths. For more detail, fold once more to make eighths. Unfold it and notice the center point and the equal sections, like slices of a pie.
3
Remember radial balance. Everything will radiate out from the center. Whatever you draw in one section will repeat in all the others.
4
Design ONE section. In just one section, pencil a few simple shapes and lines: petals, curves, triangles, circles, or leaves. Let some of them touch the edges of the section.
5
Transfer your design to the next section. Fold the next section over your drawing and trace firmly so a faint copy presses through onto it. Open it back up and trace over the faint lines so they are clear. Repeat this around the circle.
6
Complete the mandala so your design repeats in every section. Now the whole circle shows radial balance.
7
Pick your best side. Choose the cleanest side of the paper to color.
8
Choose 4 to 5 colors that work well together. Repeat the same colors around the circle so the design feels like one whole (this is unity).
9
Color carefully. Press firmly and fill each section neatly. If you like, outline your shapes with a darker color so they stand out.
10
Add final details and sign your work. Make sure your patterns repeat evenly and radiate from the center. Then sign your name — every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
⭐ WHAT MAKES A STRONG ARTWORK
✅ The design repeats evenly in every section (radial balance).
✅ A clear pattern of shapes circles the center.
✅ 4 to 5 colors repeat around the circle for unity.
✅ Color is applied with care; no big empty gaps.
✅ The work is signed.
✍️ ARTIST STATEMENT (type this in the submission box)
In 1–2 sentences, in your own voice, tell us about your mandala:
• What shapes did you repeat, and why did you choose them?
• Which part of building radial balance was the hardest to get right?
• What are you proud of in this design?

Elements & Principles Clear radial balance; pattern repeats evenly all around Mostly balanced; minor uneven spots Balance or repetition is uneven in places Little radial balance or repeating pattern
Craftsmanship & Technique Neat lines; full, careful color; clean transfers Competent; minor neatness issues Uneven; rushed in places Little care or effort
Creative Problem-Solving Original shapes and color choices throughout Some original thinking Follows steps, little personal voice Minimal engagement
Artist Statement Specific, personal, uses art vocabulary Clear, some specificity Vague or general Minimal or missing
Completion & Signature Complete; design fills the circle; signed Mostly complete; signed Partially complete Incomplete and/or unsigned
Total: 100 pts

✏️ PURPOSE
This sketch is your warm-up rung before the big drawing. You will practice the one move the Taj Mahal project depends on: drawing half a shape, then mirroring it so both halves match. This is bilateral symmetry, the kind of balance the Taj Mahal is famous for. Focus on effort, not perfection.

Can you make the right half of a shape match the left half closely enough that the fold line looks like a mirror?

Take one sheet of paper and fold it in half the long way (top to bottom), then open it. The crease is your center line.

Now mirror it. On the other side of the center line, draw the matching half so the two sides line up: the dome completes, the arch becomes whole, and a second tower stands the same distance from the middle. This even match is balance.
4
This should take about 20–40 minutes. Keep this sheet — it is your planning notes for the Week 2 Taj Mahal Cardboard Relief.

Taj Mahal Cardboard Relief
Major Project · 100 pts · Due end of Week 2
📋 PROJECT OVERVIEW
Now you build the Taj Mahal as a relief sculpture, a piece of art that stands out from a flat background instead of lying flat on it. You will cut matching cardboard shapes, the dome, the central arch, two smaller domes, and two minaret towers, and glue them onto a cardboard base in layers so the building rises off the surface. You will keep the left and right sides matching (bilateral symmetry), add repeating pattern to the surfaces, and use layering to create real space and depth, not just drawn space. When you finish, you will have a building that stands up and casts its own small shadows.
🎯 ELEMENTS & PRINCIPLES FOCUS
Principles of Design: Balance (bilateral symmetry), Pattern
Elements of Art: Form (a 3D relief), Space (real, layered depth)
🛠️ WHAT YOU NEED
Cardboard (a flattened cereal box or shipping box works well) · scissors · white glue · a pencil · a ruler · optional: white or cream paint or paper to cover the finished piece, and markers or cut paper for pattern details
📝 STEP-BY-STEP
1
Study the symmetry. Look again at the head-on photo of the Taj Mahal on the lesson page. Notice how the left half mirrors the right half: the dome sits in the center, and matching towers stand on each side. This even match is balance.
2
Sketch your outline. On a flat piece of cardboard, lightly pencil the symmetrical outline of the building: the central dome, the tall pointed arch below it, two smaller domes, and two minaret towers.
3
Cut matching pairs. To make left and right truly match, fold a piece of cardboard and cut through both layers at once, or cut one piece and trace around it to make its mirror twin. Cut the dome, the central arch, the two small domes, and the two minarets this way, so every left piece has a matching right piece.
4
Arrange before you glue. Lay all your pieces on a flat cardboard base, centered and balanced, until the arrangement looks right. Do not glue anything yet.
5
Glue in layers. Glue your pieces to the base one layer at a time, some pieces stacked on top of others, so the building rises up off the base instead of lying flat. This layering is what makes your artwork a relief, and it is what creates space, a real sense of depth you can see from the side.
6
Add pattern. Draw or cut small repeating shapes (arches, stripes, diamonds) onto the surfaces and borders. Match the pattern on the left side to the pattern on the right. Repeating shapes create pattern.
7
Optional: finish the surface. If you like, cover the cardboard in white or cream paint or paper, like the real marble.
8
Check your balance and sign your work. Make sure the two halves match, the pattern repeats on both sides, and the layers clearly rise off the base. Then sign the back of your work — every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

✅ The left and right halves clearly mirror each other (balance).
✅ The pieces are layered so the building clearly rises off the base, creating real space and depth (relief).
✅ A repeating pattern appears on the surfaces, matched on both sides.
✅ Pieces are cut and glued neatly.
✅ The work is complete and signed.

WEEK 2 · ARTWORK + ARTIST STATEMENT
Dot Painting
Major Project · 100 pts · Due end of Week 2
📋 PROJECT OVERVIEW
Now you put texture and pattern to work in one bold artwork of your own design. You will draw an Australian animal in the center, then build a rich, dotted background around it with rows of dots, curving pathways, and your own circle and spiral motifs in warm earth tones. When you finish, you will have a striking painting that shows you can build texture and pattern dot by dot.
🙏 RESPECTFUL USE
Use the visual language (dots, concentric circles, pathways) to make your own design. Do not copy a real sacred or secret-sacred symbol; those meanings belong to the communities who hold them.
🎯 ELEMENTS & PRINCIPLES FOCUS
Element of Art: Texture (built from closely placed dots)
Principle of Design: Pattern (repeating dots, circles, and pathways)
Supporting: Movement (dots along curved lines) and Contrast (dark animal against the patterned background)
🛠️ WHAT YOU NEED
Drawing or painting paper · pencil · eraser · black marker or paint for outlining · cotton swabs or dotting tools · paint or markers in earth tones (red, brown, yellow, orange, black, white)
📝 STEP-BY-STEP
1
Choose your animal. Pick one Australian animal: a lizard, gecko, turtle, kangaroo, or snake. Draw it large in the center of your paper.
2
Outline and fill the animal. Outline it boldly in black, then fill the inside dark so it reads as one strong shape.
3
Dot around the outline. Using cotton swabs or dotting tools, place dots closely and evenly all the way around the animal's edge.
4
Draw pathways. Add wavy, curved pathway lines that flow through the background around the animal.
5
Add your own motifs. Draw a few simple circle and spiral motifs in the background. These are your designs, not copied sacred symbols.
6
Fill the background with dots. Fill the background sections with repeated dots that follow your curved lines. This builds movement, texture, and pattern. Use earth tones: red, brown, yellow, orange, black, and white.
7
Add concentric circles. In a few areas, draw concentric circles (circles inside circles), then fill around them with dots and lines.
8
Edge the animal. Add small bright dots along the inside edge of the animal so it stands out from the background.
9
Separate the sections. Use warm and cool colors to separate areas of the background. Keep the animal dark so it stays the focus against the patterned background.
10
Final touches, then sign your work. Fill any empty spaces with dots and pattern, keep your dots neat and repeated, and make sure the animal is still the focus. Then sign your name, every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
⭐ WHAT MAKES A STRONG ARTWORK
✅ A bold Australian animal fills the center, dark and outlined in black.
✅ Closely placed dots build a rich, even texture around the animal and across the background.
✅ Repeating dots, pathways, and your own circle and spiral motifs create clear pattern and movement.
✅ Earth tones fill the work, with the dark animal standing out in contrast.
✅ Empty spaces are filled, the dots are neat, and the work is signed.
✍️ ARTIST STATEMENT (type this in the submission box)
In 1–2 sentences, in your own voice, tell us about your dot painting:
• Which animal did you choose, and which part of building the texture was the most fun?
• Which step took the most patience?
• What are you proud of in this painting?
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1)
Elements & Principles Rich texture and varied pattern throughout; clear movement and contrast Texture and pattern present; minor gaps Texture or pattern is weak or barely used Little texture or pattern attempted
Craftsmanship & Technique Neat, even dots; bold outline; full, careful color Competent; minor neatness issues Uneven dots; rushed in places Little care or effort
Creative Problem-Solving Original animal and motifs throughout Some original thinking Follows steps, little personal voice Minimal engagement
Artist Statement Specific, personal, uses art vocabulary Clear, some specificity Vague or general Minimal or missing
Completion & Signature Complete; animal, background, and motifs done; signed Mostly complete; signed Partially complete Incomplete and/or unsigned
Total: 100 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: M15 · Dot Painting + Artist Statement
Photograph your finished painting in good light and upload it as a JPG or PNG. Type your Artist Statement in the submission text box.
Save a copy to your art portfolio folder in OneDrive (name it VisualArt1_M15_Artwork_YourName).
Due: End of Week 2. You built texture and pattern dot by dot, be proud of it.

Build a Standing Totem
Major Project · 100 pts · Due end of Week 2
📋 PROJECT OVERVIEW
Now you put form, symbolism, and balance to work in three dimensions. Instead of gluing cut-paper shapes flat on a sheet, you will stack 3 or 4 cut-paper figures, animals or symbols, onto a standing base such as a cardboard tube, a small box, or a stack of cups, building upward from bottom to top. This is an original design inspired by the Northwest Coast tradition, made respectfully, not a copy of any one tribe's crest. When you finish, you will have a standing totem of your own, each figure carrying a symbol you chose.
🎯 ELEMENTS & PRINCIPLES FOCUS
Element of Art: Form (a real three-dimensional, standing construction)
Big idea: Symbolism (each stacked figure stands for a trait or story you connect with)
Principles of Design: Balance / symmetry and Pattern
🛠️ WHAT YOU NEED
A paper towel tube, a small box, or a stack of cups (choose one for your base) · construction paper or colored paper (several colors) · scissors · glue or tape · coloring tools · your Week 1 sketch and colored plan
📝 STEP-BY-STEP
1
Remember what totem poles are. They are carved cedar monuments made by Northwest Coast peoples, such as the Haida, Tlingit, and Kwakwaka'wakw, with several figures stacked one above another. Each figure stands for a family, story, or trait. Keep that idea of a stacked symbol in mind.
2
Plan your stacked figures. Choose 3 or 4 animals or symbols, one for each level of your totem, from bottom to top. Decide what trait or story each one stands for, using your Week 1 sketch as a starting point.
3
Choose your base. Pick one: a paper towel tube, a small box, or a stack of cups.
4
Cut symmetrical shapes. For each figure, fold a piece of paper, draw half of a shape against the fold, and cut it out so it opens into a balanced, matching shape.
5
Build upward. Starting at the bottom, wrap or attach each figure's shapes around your base, working your way up to the top, one figure at a time.
6
Add parts that stick out. Cut and add wings, beaks, ears, or noses that stand away from the base, so your totem reads as a real three-dimensional standing form.
7
Color, pattern, and sign. Add color and a repeating pattern to each figure. Check that your totem stands on its own, then sign the base; every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
⭐ WHAT MAKES A STRONG ARTWORK
✅ 3 or 4 figures are stacked from bottom to top on a standing base.
✅ Each figure is symmetrical and balanced, left and right.
✅ Parts stick out (wings, beaks, ears, or noses) for a real three-dimensional effect.
✅ Color and a repeating pattern are added with care.
✅ The totem stands on its own, and the base is signed.
✍️ ARTIST STATEMENT (type this in the submission box)
In 1–2 sentences, in your own voice, tell us about your totem animal:
• Which animal did you choose, and what trait does it stand for?
• How did you use symmetry to balance your design?
• What are you proud of in this standing totem?

Craftsmanship & Technique Clean cuts; flat, neatly glued, layered shapes Competent; minor neatness issues Uneven cuts or curling pieces Little care or effort
Creative Problem-Solving Original animal and meaningful symbol throughout Some original thinking Follows steps, little personal voice Minimal engagement
Artist Statement Specific, personal, uses art vocabulary Clear, some specificity Vague or general Minimal or missing
Completion & Signature Complete standing totem; details added; signed Mostly complete; signed Partially complete Incomplete and/or unsigned
Total: 100 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Design Your Own Glyph Block

📋 PROJECT OVERVIEW
Now you become the scribe. You will design your own short "inscription" out of glyph blocks, inspired by the Maya style. You will invent your own symbols, pack them into rounded blocks, and arrange them like a Maya carving. When you finish, you will have one bold design that is both writing and art, made entirely by you.
📝 Important: You are inventing your own symbols in the Maya style. You are not copying real Maya glyphs or their meanings. Real glyphs carried specific words and sounds that scholars study carefully. Your block borrows the look (rounded shapes, packed blocks), but the meanings are yours.
👀 GLYPH EXAMPLES TO STUDY
Here are eight real Maya glyph blocks to choose from. Look closely at a few before you begin: notice the rounded-square shape, the packed faces and scrolls, and how little empty space is left. Pick two or three whose look you like, and let them guide the style of your own invented blocks (not the meaning).
🎯 ELEMENTS & PRINCIPLES FOCUS
Principles of Design: Symbol & Pattern (with Balance supporting)
Element of Art: Shape (rounded blocks, scrolls, ovals, circles)
🛠️ WHAT YOU NEED
Drawing paper · pencil · eraser · black marker or pen for outlining · earth-tone coloring tools (browns, tans, ochre, rust) or a gray pencil for a carved-stone look
📝 STEP-BY-STEP
1
Study real Maya glyphs. Look again at the carvings from the lesson and at the eight glyph examples above. Notice the rounded square "blocks" packed with faces, shapes, and small marks, with almost no empty space.
2
Choose a short idea to represent. Pick something small: your initials, a single word, or a personal symbol like "courage" or "family." This is what your blocks will stand for.
3
Sketch your blocks. Lightly draw 2 to 4 glyph blocks as rounded squares. Round the corners, just like the Maya.
4
Fill each block with your own symbols. Invent your own stylized faces, shapes, and small marks inspired by the Maya style. Pack each block full and balanced. These are your inventions, not copies of real Maya glyph meanings.
5
Arrange the blocks like a Maya inscription. Stack them in a single column, or set them in a 2-wide grid, so they read as one tidy unit.
6

7
Add color or shading. Color with earth tones (browns, tans, ochre, rust), or shade in gray so the blocks look like carved stone.
8

WEEK 2 · ARTWORK + ARTIST STATEMENT
My Own Sun Stone
Major Project · 100 pts · Due end of Week 2
📋 PROJECT OVERVIEW
Now you put radial balance to work in your own artwork. Like the Aztec carvers, you will start at a bold face in the center of a circle, then build rings of repeated symbols outward to the edge so the whole design radiates evenly. You will outline it boldly and color it in warm colors. When you finish, you will have a single bold round design that proves you can balance a picture around a center.
🎯 ELEMENTS & PRINCIPLES FOCUS
Principles of Design: Radial Balance (the design radiates evenly from a center)
Supporting: Symbol, Pattern, Contrast, and warm Color
🛠️ WHAT YOU NEED
Drawing paper · pencil · eraser · a round object to trace (bowl or plate) · black marker or pen for outlining · warm-color tools (yellow, orange, red, gold, brown colored pencils, crayons, or markers)
📝 STEP-BY-STEP
1
Study the Sun Stone again. Look back at the lesson image: a face in the center, then rings of symbols radiating outward to the edge. That is the plan you will follow.
2
Draw a large circle. Trace a bowl or plate so your circle fills most of the page. Bigger is better.
3
Draw a bold face in the exact center. Keep it simple and large enough to be the clear middle of your design. This is where every ring will begin.
4
Add concentric rings around the face. Draw two or three more circles around the center face. Divide each ring into repeated sections or symbols, spaced evenly, so the design radiates the same way all the way around (this is your radial balance).
5
Add a ring of sun rays or points around the outer edge, reaching outward, so the whole design feels like a sun shining in every direction.
6
Outline boldly in black. Trace the face, the rings, and the symbols with marker or pen so every part stands out clearly.
7
Color with warm colors. Use only yellow, orange, red, gold, and brown. Alternate the colors around each ring so the pattern pops, and place darker warm tones (deep red, brown) next to lighter ones (yellow, gold) for contrast.
8
Final touches and sign your work. Fill all the spaces, keep it bold and complete, then sign your name — every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
⭐ WHAT MAKES A STRONG ARTWORK
✅ A bold face sits in the exact center, with rings radiating evenly around it.
✅ Symbols repeat at even spaces, so the design balances any way you turn it.
✅ The circle is large and fills the page.
✅ Everything is outlined boldly so the design is clear.
✅ Warm colors alternate, with dark warm tones next to light ones for contrast; no big empty white gaps.
✅ The work is signed.
✍️ ARTIST STATEMENT (type this in the submission box)

• What did you put in the center, and what do your symbols stand for?
• How did you keep your rings radiating evenly around the center?
• What are you proud of in this design?
